prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates the seated man in frames 1–2 as the nearest large surface, roughly 0.6–1.0 m in front of the camera, with the chair and couch immediately behind him and the lamp and rear furniture about 1.5–3 m away. As the camera turns downward and right in frames 3–5, nearby arms, hands, legs, and the tabletop/floor region appear within roughly 0.2–1 m, while the room background recedes beyond about 2 m; this depth ordering and the extent of foreground occlusion are clearer than in RGB. The man initially faces and appears to look toward the camera, but later is mostly above, right of, or partly outside the view as the viewpoint rotates. The map is unreliable for exact metre estimates, merges some neighboring surfaces, and gives inconsistent brightness around limbs, furniture edges, and the bright phone screen.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies a person directly ahead in frames 1–2, with a chair behind and to his right, another chair farther right, and a couch to the left; the person partly occludes the seating behind him. In frame 3, only a partly visible person occupies the upper area, while in frame 4 a large person mask fills the right foreground and a cell phone lies left of that person, apparently within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach and roughly 0.5–1 m from the other person. Frame 5 separates overlapping person regions across the lower and right portions of the view, showing that bodies or arms are very close and partly out of frame, though it cannot reliably distinguish all limbs or determine which visible body parts belong together. This map makes object identity and overlap clearer than RGB, but it misses much of the furniture and small objects, fragments people near boundaries, and provides no dependable metric distance by itself.
descriptions.pose: The pose map shows a seated upper-body configuration in frames 1–2, centered slightly left and facing approximately toward the camera, with the head above the shoulders and bent arms extending downward; this clarifies body orientation despite the chair and torso overlap in RGB. In frame 3 the body estimate breaks into sparse clusters near the upper-middle area as the camera turns downward, so orientation and separation from the camera wearer become uncertain. Frame 4 contains a magenta hand outline near the upper center-right, about arm’s length from the viewpoint, while frame 5 shows overlapping hand keypoints near the center-right and a large yellow limb polygon extending toward the right edge, indicating very close, partly cropped limbs. The skeleton map exposes joint and hand geometry that is difficult to trace in RGB, but it is unreliable where people are truncated, motion-blurred, occluded, or extremely close, and some yellow shapes may join incorrect keypoints.
